title: mantra sadhana (a 40-day japa discipline)
hook: a yoga Upanishad hears a mantra in the breath itself, one nobody has to say

segments.voice: Yesterday, mantra sadhana at dawn and dusk: standing until the sun shows, sitting until the stars appear.

Ha, on the way out. Sa, on the way in. Breathe out slowly through the nose, and the air makes a soft sound, close to an h. Breathe in, and there's a faint hiss, close to an s. Easy to miss; it's just breath. But some yoga texts heard something more. To them, that soft sound was a mantra, repeated day and night by every breathing creature, without anyone choosing to say it.
screen: `HA, ON THE WAY OUT.` → `SA, ON THE WAY IN.` → `A MANTRA NOBODY SAYS.`

segments.voice: The text is the Dhyanabindu Upanishad, one of the yoga Upanishads. In paraphrase: the breath goes out with the sound ha and comes back in with the sound sa, and so the living being is always repeating hamsa, hamsa. This, it says, is called the ajapa gayatri. Ajapa means not-japa, or japa that isn't done: repetition that happens without effort, with no beads, no lips, no count. Hamsa is also the Sanskrit word for a swan or a wild goose, a bird some texts use as a picture of the soul. Some teachers turn the sound around: so'ham, which can be heard as I am that. Either way, in this teaching a mantra is already going on in every breathing body, and the practice is to notice it. Here the last two blocks meet. Pranayama sequences worked with the breath; mantra sadhana works with the sound. In this teaching they turn out to be one thing. That changes how a long sadhana can feel. For four days the practice has been about keeping something going: setting terms, counting beads, tying it to dawn and dusk. Ajapa says something quieter. The repetition isn't only the one you push. It's also the one you finally hear. Some teachers who use this keep the beads and the chosen mantra, and let the mantra ride on the breath, one sound on the out-breath, one on the in, until it's hard to tell which is carrying which. The discipline stays: the terms, the beads, the hinge of the day. It just rides on a sound the breath was already making.
screen: `HA OUT, SA IN: HAMSA.` · `AJAPA: THE JAPA NOT DONE.` · `THE BREATH AND THE MANTRA MEET.` · `THE REPETITION YOU HEAR.`

segments.voice: Let the breath move through the nose, no counting, and listen: a soft ha on the out-breath, a faint sa on the in, not made any louder. If you've been keeping a mantra, let it rest on that sound, part on the out-breath and part on the in; if not, stay with hamsa, or with the breath's own sound. When the mind drifts, come back to listening.
Mantra sadhana. A mantra kept as a discipline. Today, ajapa: the mantra the breath keeps by itself, ha out and sa in, waiting to be heard.
Your line: one mantra, day after day. Some days it's kept going, and some days it's simply heard. Day one thousand sixteen, done.

howItsDone: Some Hindu yoga teachers teach ajapa japa, listening to the breath's own sound as hamsa or so'ham and letting a chosen mantra move with the in-breath and out-breath.

chat.says: What's the 'mantra nobody says' that some yoga texts talk about?
options: Hamsa: ha as you breathe out, sa as you breathe in, said by the breath itself.
The last word of a long chant, which everyone leaves out on purpose.
A mantra written on paper and kept in a drawer, never spoken.
